goldens.comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.

The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13 — A matching blocked address is not counted whenever the whitelist/blacklist has already added an email error, leaving persistent blocked-email metrics blind to those attempts.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at lib/validators/email_validator.rb lines 4-14, the logic is: first check whitelist (lines 4-7), then check blacklist (lines 8-11), and only if no errors exist yet (line 13: 'if record.errors[attribute].blank?'), check BlockedEmail.should_block?. This means if an email is rejected by whitelist/blacklist rules, the BlockedEmail.should_block? method is never called, so the match_count and last_match_at statistics in the blocked_emails table won't be updated for those attempts. This is a real bug where blocked email metrics are incomplete when other validation rules fire first.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13 — The registration path calls `user.valid?` before `user.save`, so each rejected attempt increments match_count twice.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real issue. Looking at the diff, `BlockedEmail.should_block?` (lines 11-18 in blocked_email.rb) increments `match_count` every time it's called for a matching email. The EmailValidator calls this method in `validate_each`. In Rails, when you call both `user.valid?` and then `user.save` (which also runs validations), the validator runs twice, causing `match_count` to be incremented twice per registration attempt. This is a legitimate bug in the statistics tracking logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — Concurrent validations read and save match_count non-atomically, losing blocked-email match increments.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows in app/models/blocked_email.rb lines 12-17 that should_block? performs a read-modify-write sequence: it reads the record, increments match_count in memory, then saves. This is a classic race condition - if two concurrent requests check the same email, both read the same match_count value, both increment it to the same new value, and both save, losing one increment. This is a real correctness bug in the new code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb:5 — action_type` is NOT NULL but has no database default, so data loads or inserts that bypass model callbacks fail instead of defaulting to `block`.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the migration creates action_type as NOT NULL without a database default (line 5: `t.integer :action_type, null: false`). While the model has a `before_validation :set_defaults` callback that sets `self.action_type ||= BlockedEmail.actions[:block]`, this only works when records are created through ActiveRecord with validations. Direct SQL inserts, bulk data loads, or any operation that bypasses model callbacks would fail with a NOT NULL constraint violation. This is a real defect in the schema design.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/users_controller.rb:198 — The signup API exposes raw model errors and attributes only to drive an Ember branch, coupling its response contract to model internals.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the users_controller.rb change at line 198 exposes user.errors.to_hash and user.attributes.slice() in the API response. This is specifically done to support the Ember frontend's rejectedEmails feature (visible in create_account_controller.js). While this is a valid architectural concern about coupling the API contract to model internals, it's not a bug - it's a design decision that could make future refactoring harder. The finding is grounded in specific diff lines and raises a legitimate concern about API design.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:12 — Each validation loads and saves a matching row, and create calls validation twice so blocked signups cause two reads and two writes.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real issue. Looking at the diff, `BlockedEmail.should_block?` is called from `EmailValidator.validate_each` (line 13 of email_validator.rb). The `should_block?` method performs a database read and, if a record is found, increments `match_count` and saves the record. In Rails, validation typically runs twice during `create` (once for `valid?` check and once during save), which would cause duplicate reads and writes. This is a legitimate performance/correctness concern - the match_count would be incremented twice per blocked signup attempt.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:12 — Exact case-sensitive blocked-email lookup lets signup requests bypass a block by changing email casing.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows BlockedEmail.should_block? uses an exact match query: `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`. Email addresses are case-insensitive by RFC standards, but this query performs a case-sensitive lookup in most databases. A user could bypass a block on 'bad@spammer.com' by signing up with 'BAD@spammer.com'. The EmailValidator calls BlockedEmail.should_block?(value) with the raw email value, so case variations would not match blocked entries.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb:11 — The validator specs stub `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, so they never verify that a persisted blocked email rejects a real User validation.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the email_validator_spec.rb stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? rather than using actual persisted BlockedEmail records. While spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb does test the should_block? method with real records, there's no integration test that verifies the full flow from User validation through EmailValidator to BlockedEmail with persisted data. This is a valid test coverage concern - the validator tests use stubs, so they don't verify the actual integration works correctly. However, this is a test completeness issue, not a bug, since the individual components are tested.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:274 — No client test covers a failed registration response marking the returned email invalid and clearing that state when the address changes.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new client-side logic at line 274 that pushes rejected emails to an array when registration fails with email errors, and this array is used in email validation (lines 68-73). The finding correctly identifies that there are no client-side tests added for this new functionality. The diff only shows server-side Ruby specs (email_validator_spec.rb, blocked_email_spec.rb) but no JavaScript tests for the create_account_controller changes. This is a legitimate concern about missing test coverage for newly added nontrivial logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/users_controller.rb:195 — No controller/request test asserts the new failure-response `errors` and `values` contract consumed by the signup controller.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows new JSON response fields 'errors' and 'values' being added to the users_controller.rb failure response (lines 197-199), and the JavaScript controller consuming these fields (lines 273-275). The finding correctly identifies that while there are model specs for BlockedEmail and validator specs for EmailValidator, there are no controller/request tests in this diff that verify the new API contract. This is a legitimate test coverage gap for newly added functionality.
